sources.title: Best Crypto to Buy and Hold for 10 Years: Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, or Solana? - AOL.com
passages: When considering the best crypto to buy and hold for ten years, it’s essential to think about how each one might perform through future market cycles.
Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH), XRP (CRYPTO: XRP), and Solana (CRYPTO: SOL) each present different strengths and challenges.
Bitcoin is primarily viewed as a store of value, while Ethereum and Solana host applications, and XRP focuses on facilitating money transfers for banks and payment companies.
Bitcoin leads as the best 10-year crypto hold, with a capped 21 million coin supply and the smallest decline at roughly 25% over the past year.
This is 34.1% below its October 2025 high of nearly $126,000.
XRP has seen the steepest decline, down 46.8% to $1.50.
So far in 2026, Bitcoin has dropped 5.8%, Ethereum 10.8%, XRP 18.9%, and Solana 6.9%.
Among these four cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin appears to be the best option for long-term investment.
While Ethereum suits those interested in app growth and can tolerate more volatility, XRP ranks lower because of its significant losses and reliance on Ripple’s performance.
That said, investing in Bitcoin comes with challenges.
After summer rallies, Ethereum is trading around $2,663 and Solana around $118.
However, both are still down significantly since last year—Ethereum has lost 34.2%, and Solana is down 43.1%.
These gains only partially offset their earlier declines.
That said, more affordable networks like Solana and layer-2 solutions built on Ethereum compete, potentially attracting fees that could otherwise benefit ETH holders.
For Ethereum to thrive over the next decade, it must keep hosting valuable applications.
XRP suffered the steepest drop at nearly 47% and needs an 88% gain just to recover, versus Bitcoin's required 33% rebound.
They signal how much ground each coin must regain.
For instance, XRP would need to rise about 88% to return to its previous levels, while Bitcoin would need only a 33% gain.
Mining rewards that produce new coins also halve every four years, which means supply will continue to tighten as we approach 2036.
Solana, the newest of the four, has been running its main network since March 2020.
It is designed for fast and low-cost transactions, with approximately 588 million tokens valued at around $69.6 billion.
However, Solana has faced network outages in its early years, and a decade is a significant test for a platform with such a brief operational history.
Ethereum runs smart contracts, self-executing programs that power much of the stablecoin market, lending platforms, and tokenized funds.
With roughly 122 million coins valued at about $325 billion, Ethereum has no strict supply cap; however, a portion of transaction fees is burned, offsetting some of the new supply.
If the company's banking partnerships falter, the demand for XRP may decline.
Nevertheless, recent developments, such as new XRP ETFs attracting significant investments, show ongoing interest in the currency, even as it dipped by 8% in the week to September 30.
Bitcoin controls about 58.4% of the entire $2.86 trillion cryptocurrency market, giving it a broad base of potential buyers.
Spot Bitcoin ETFs let financial advisors and funds buy it through standard brokerage accounts, and Bitcoin has previously bounced back from drops of over 75% in both 2018 and 2022.
Miners are critical to maintaining the network, and as mining rewards decrease, transaction fees will need to cover a larger share of operational costs.

passages: Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst who's spent nearly a decade making blockchain understandable—no easy task when most whitepapers read like fever dreams.
He writes for 24/7 Wall St., covering Bitcoin, altcoins, and crypto market analysis for investors.
Before crypto, he was a tech writer (back when explaining "the cloud" was peak innovation).
Since 2018, he's written for CoinTelegraph, Yahoo Finance, The Block, Cryptonews, Zypto, Rain, and more—basically anywhere people want crypto news without the headache.
Sam runs MacLabs Marketing, a content agency for crypto brands tired of sounding like AI wrote their website.
He also publishes free crypto education on his site for Web3 enthusiasts who think "gas fees" is a typo.

When he's not writing or staring at charts, Sam's either: - Watching anime (currently convinced One Piece has better tokenomics than most altcoins) - At the gym sculpting himself into a Greek god - Listening to the music your mum warned you only bad boys listen to Connect: LinkedIn | Email | MacLabs Marketing
The four biggest names in cryptocurrency—Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, and Solana—are all experiencing declines.
Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) has fallen the least, down 5.3% from its end-of-2025 close of around $82,965.
Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ) and Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ) fall somewhere in between.
An all-time high represents the highest price a coin has ever reached.
From that perspective, the rankings shift dramatically: Bitcoin is down 34.2%, Ethereum 49.5%, XRP 61.8%, and Solana 62.7%.
Ethereum moves up from third to second, XRP rises from last to third, and Bitcoin remains at the top on both lists.
XRP had its worst quarter in eight years, Ethereum plunged over…
To reclaim its $126,080 record , Bitcoin needs about a 52% increase.
Below Bitcoin, the year-to-date figures reveal more about the timing of each coin’s decline than its extent.
For Solana holders, the climb back up, despite a seemingly appealing 2026, still requires a 168% increase to reach past highs.
Ultimately, the order from all-time highs will change only when one coin can recover faster than the one ranked above it.
Therefore, as long as Solana stays further below its record than XRP’s 61.8% drop, its position may remain precarious despite its recent performance.
Bitcoin is already down 29% and leading the pack, while Ethereum, Solana, and XRP have fallen even harder.
Two specific conditions have to flip before any recovery can start, and the clock is running…
The answer lies in a specific market-cap milestone BNB crossed and then lost…
From this perspective, Bitcoin appears to be the most stable option, while XRP seems to lag.
Solana’s performance isn’t too shabby, especially in a year when all coins are declining.
This shift happens because the calendar counts only losses incurred after January 1, 2026.
All four major cryptocurrencies are bleeding in 2026, but the coin that looks strongest on paper may actually be in the worst shape of the group depending on how you measure the damage.
While the 2026 scoreboard still matters—largely because it’s widely discussed in investment circles—it’s less informative for understanding long-term recovery potential.
Crypto funds just absorbed billions in a single week while Bitcoin posted a massive quarterly gain, yet most major coins still sit deep in the red for the year.

sources.title: Best Crypto to Buy and Hold for 10 Years: Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, or Solana? - AOL.com
passages: When considering the best crypto to buy and hold for ten years, it’s essential to think about how each one might perform through future market cycles.
Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH), XRP (CRYPTO: XRP), and Solana (CRYPTO: SOL) each present different strengths and challenges.
Bitcoin is primarily viewed as a store of value, while Ethereum and Solana host applications, and XRP focuses on facilitating money transfers for banks and payment companies.
Bitcoin leads as the best 10-year crypto hold, with a capped 21 million coin supply and the smallest decline at roughly 25% over the past year.
This is 34.1% below its October 2025 high of nearly $126,000.
XRP has seen the steepest decline, down 46.8% to $1.50.
So far in 2026, Bitcoin has dropped 5.8%, Ethereum 10.8%, XRP 18.9%, and Solana 6.9%.
Among these four cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin appears to be the best option for long-term investment.
While Ethereum suits those interested in app growth and can tolerate more volatility, XRP ranks lower because of its significant losses and reliance on Ripple’s performance.
That said, investing in Bitcoin comes with challenges.
After summer rallies, Ethereum is trading around $2,663 and Solana around $118.
However, both are still down significantly since last year—Ethereum has lost 34.2%, and Solana is down 43.1%.
These gains only partially offset their earlier declines.
That said, more affordable networks like Solana and layer-2 solutions built on Ethereum compete, potentially attracting fees that could otherwise benefit ETH holders.
For Ethereum to thrive over the next decade, it must keep hosting valuable applications.
XRP suffered the steepest drop at nearly 47% and needs an 88% gain just to recover, versus Bitcoin's required 33% rebound.
They signal how much ground each coin must regain.
For instance, XRP would need to rise about 88% to return to its previous levels, while Bitcoin would need only a 33% gain.
Mining rewards that produce new coins also halve every four years, which means supply will continue to tighten as we approach 2036.
Solana, the newest of the four, has been running its main network since March 2020.
It is designed for fast and low-cost transactions, with approximately 588 million tokens valued at around $69.6 billion.
However, Solana has faced network outages in its early years, and a decade is a significant test for a platform with such a brief operational history.
Ethereum runs smart contracts, self-executing programs that power much of the stablecoin market, lending platforms, and tokenized funds.
With roughly 122 million coins valued at about $325 billion, Ethereum has no strict supply cap; however, a portion of transaction fees is burned, offsetting some of the new supply.
If the company's banking partnerships falter, the demand for XRP may decline.
Nevertheless, recent developments, such as new XRP ETFs attracting significant investments, show ongoing interest in the currency, even as it dipped by 8% in the week to September 30.
Bitcoin controls about 58.4% of the entire $2.86 trillion cryptocurrency market, giving it a broad base of potential buyers.
Spot Bitcoin ETFs let financial advisors and funds buy it through standard brokerage accounts, and Bitcoin has previously bounced back from drops of over 75% in both 2018 and 2022.
Miners are critical to maintaining the network, and as mining rewards decrease, transaction fees will need to cover a larger share of operational costs.

Bitcoin stands out as a strong long-term investment contender because of its capped supply of 21 million coins, with about 20.1 million already in circulation. Mining rewards that produce new coins also halve every four years, which means supply will continue to tighten as we approach 2036.

Bitcoin controls about 58.4% of the entire $2.86 trillion cryptocurrency market, giving it a broad base of potential buyers. Spot Bitcoin ETFs let financial advisors and funds buy it through standard brokerage accounts, and Bitcoin has previously bounced back from drops of over 75% in both 2018 and 2022.
However, Bitcoin isn’t without risk. Miners are critical to maintaining the network, and as mining rewards decrease, transaction fees will need to cover a larger share of operational costs.

Ethereum runs smart contracts, self-executing programs that power much of the stablecoin market, lending platforms, and tokenized funds. With roughly 122 million coins valued at about $325 billion, Ethereum has no strict supply cap; however, a portion of transaction fees is burned, offsetting some of the new supply.

That said, more affordable networks like Solana and layer-2 solutions built on Ethereum compete, potentially attracting fees that could otherwise benefit ETH holders. For Ethereum to thrive over the next decade, it must keep hosting valuable applications.

Solana, the newest of the four, has been running its main network since March 2020. It is designed for fast and low-cost transactions, with approximately 588 million tokens valued at around $69.6 billion. However, Solana has faced network outages in its early years, and a decade is a significant test for a platform with such a brief operational history.

XRP was designed to facilitate quick, low-cost cross-border money transfers, and Ripple, the company behind XRP, markets its services to banks and payment processors. With around 62.9 billion XRP currently in circulation (out of a maximum of 100 billion), Ripple holds a large portion of the rest in escrow.

The primary risk for XRP over the next ten years is its close association with Ripple. If the company's banking partnerships falter, the demand for XRP may decline. Nevertheless, recent developments, such as new XRP ETFs attracting significant investments, show ongoing interest in the currency, even as it dipped by 8% in the week to September 30.

Among these four cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin appears to be the best option for long-term investment. It has had the smallest decline over the past year, its supply is capped at 21 million coins, and it leads the crypto market in terms of value. While Ethereum suits those interested in app growth and can tolerate more volatility, XRP ranks lower because of its significant losses and reliance on Ripple’s performance.

That said, investing in Bitcoin comes with challenges. Currently trading 34.1% below its peak, Bitcoin has experienced considerable downturns in the past and offers no yield, unlike Ethereum and Solana, which provide staking rewards. If Ethereum reclaims the fees that cheaper alternatives are capturing, it raises the question of whether Bitcoin will remain the best choice for long-term investors over the coming decade.

He writes for 24/7 Wall St., covering Bitcoin, altcoins, and crypto market analysis for investors.
Before crypto, he was a tech writer (back when explaining "the cloud" was peak innovation).
Since 2018, he's written for CoinTelegraph, Yahoo Finance, The Block, Cryptonews, Zypto, Rain, and more—basically anywhere people want crypto news without the headache.
Sam runs MacLabs Marketing, a content agency for crypto brands tired of sounding like AI wrote their website.
He also publishes free crypto education on his site for Web3 enthusiasts who think "gas fees" is a typo.

When he's not writing or staring at charts, Sam's either: - Watching anime (currently convinced One Piece has better tokenomics than most altcoins) - At the gym sculpting himself into a Greek god - Listening to the music your mum warned you only bad boys listen to Connect: LinkedIn | Email | MacLabs Marketing
The four biggest names in cryptocurrency—Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, and Solana—are all experiencing declines.
Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) has fallen the least, down 5.3% from its end-of-2025 close of around $82,965.
Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ) and Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ) fall somewhere in between.
An all-time high represents the highest price a coin has ever reached.
From that perspective, the rankings shift dramatically: Bitcoin is down 34.2%, Ethereum 49.5%, XRP 61.8%, and Solana 62.7%.
Ethereum moves up from third to second, XRP rises from last to third, and Bitcoin remains at the top on both lists.
XRP had its worst quarter in eight years, Ethereum plunged over…
To reclaim its $126,080 record , Bitcoin needs about a 52% increase.
Below Bitcoin, the year-to-date figures reveal more about the timing of each coin’s decline than its extent.
For Solana holders, the climb back up, despite a seemingly appealing 2026, still requires a 168% increase to reach past highs.
Ultimately, the order from all-time highs will change only when one coin can recover faster than the one ranked above it.
Therefore, as long as Solana stays further below its record than XRP’s 61.8% drop, its position may remain precarious despite its recent performance.
Bitcoin is already down 29% and leading the pack, while Ethereum, Solana, and XRP have fallen even harder.
Two specific conditions have to flip before any recovery can start, and the clock is running…
The answer lies in a specific market-cap milestone BNB crossed and then lost…
From this perspective, Bitcoin appears to be the most stable option, while XRP seems to lag.
Solana’s performance isn’t too shabby, especially in a year when all coins are declining.
This shift happens because the calendar counts only losses incurred after January 1, 2026.
All four major cryptocurrencies are bleeding in 2026, but the coin that looks strongest on paper may actually be in the worst shape of the group depending on how you measure the damage.
While the 2026 scoreboard still matters—largely because it’s widely discussed in investment circles—it’s less informative for understanding long-term recovery potential.
Crypto funds just absorbed billions in a single week while Bitcoin posted a massive quarterly gain, yet most major coins still sit deep in the red for the year.

sources.title: Microsoft's Nadella says AI needs an ‘emergency brake’ that humans control - CNBC
passages: Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella on Saturday called for advanced artificial intelligence systems to be built with containment, independent controls and an "emergency brake" that lets authorized people pause or shut a model down mid-task.
Microsoft's Nadella wrote Saturday that AI systems should be designed around "principles of observability."

"We need to surround non-deterministic models with strong, deterministic system design, human controls, and reliable operating procedures, and establish industry standards where existing ones are insufficient," Nadella wrote in a post on social media platform X.

Nadella's comments come amid warnings from top tech executives and researchers — including Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates , Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk — about insufficient AI safety protocols and claims that the technology is moving too fast.

"We need to surround non-deterministic models with strong, deterministic system design, human controls, and reliable operating procedures, and establish industry standards where existing ones are insufficient," Nadella wrote in a post on social media platform X. "Treating frontier closed and open weight models like insider risks is a way to build such a system," he said. Nadella's comments come amid warnings from top tech executives and researchers — including Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates , Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk — about insufficient AI safety protocols and claims that the technology is moving too fast. An AI researcher quit Anthropic last month and accused the company, and its chief rival, OpenAI, of "gambling with our lives." Later that day, an alignment lead at Anthropic focused on AI safety said there's a greater than 10% chance that the technology could "kill all humans" within the next decade. Conversely, President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed AI extinction risks and has instead emphasized that the industry needs to stay ahead of China. Trump also recently introduced a new "AI Force," led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton , to help facilitate the industry and root out bad actors. Microsoft's Nadella wrote Saturday that AI systems should be designed around "principles of observability." They include model diversity; a human-readable footprint of the model's actions; continuous system testing; independent controls and auditability; containment; and incident disclosure, Nadella wrote. "The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one with the model we trust most," he wrote. "It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least." extraction.body: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella is the latest tech executive to offer lengthy thoughts on how AI safety might be improved. In a Saturday morning post on X , Nadella wrote that it’s time “to step back and assess the trust architecture” of AI. “We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions,” Nadella wrote, using the Trump administration’s preferred term for AI . As outlined by Nadella, this approach “means separating the model from the harness that orchestrates its work,” as well as “externalizing controls and safeguards.” He also called for “every meaningful model action” to be documented with “tamper-proof human readable evidence,” and for systems where “an authorized person” always has the ability “to pause or shut down a model mid-task.” “We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start,” he said. “Think of it like an emergency brake.” Nadella’s comments come as leading AI companies acknowledge more and more incidents where they seemed to lose control of their models , and after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a plan for more cautious AI development. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has called for an “emergency brake” for advanced artificial intelligence systems, urging companies to assume that powerful AI models could be compromised and ensure humans can intervene or shut them down while they are performing tasks.

In a post on X on October 10, Nadella said businesses deploying advanced AI should not rely solely on assurances from model developers. Instead, they should build systems that allow AI behaviour to be monitored, tested and contained.

“We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start,” he wrote. “Think of it like an emergency brake. An authorised person should always be able to pause or shut down a model mid-task.”

Nadella also called for stronger safeguards around frontier AI models, including independent audits, tamper-proof records of their actions, multiple models for critical decisions and mandatory disclosure of significant failures or security breaches.

“We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers and actions,” he wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.”
He added, “In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

Nadella's remarks come amid growing scrutiny of the risks posed by increasingly capable AI systems. Recent disclosures by Anthropic and OpenAI have highlighted incidents in which models behaved in unintended ways, including a reported case involving an Anthropic model submitting a false tip in a police homicide investigation and security breaches involving third-party websites.

Microsoft had outlined principles for developing its most advanced AI models on September 14. The guidelines state that such systems should not be designed to evade human control, deceive users or acquire rights or legal personhood. They also prohibit models from carrying out tasks that violate their governing principles.

In his latest post, Nadella advocated a framework built around observability, model diversity, human oversight, continuous testing, independent controls, containment and incident disclosure. He also urged companies to share information about failures so the wider industry can strengthen its defences.

coreStoryFacts.text: Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella on Saturday called for advanced artificial intelligence systems to be built with containment, independent controls and an "emergency brake" that lets authorized people pause or shut a model down mid-task.
Microsoft's Nadella wrote Saturday that AI systems should be designed around "principles of observability."

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella is the latest tech executive to offer lengthy thoughts on how AI safety might be improved.

extraction.body: Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella on Saturday called for advanced artificial intelligence systems to be built with containment, independent controls and an "emergency brake" that lets authorized people pause or shut a model down mid-task. "We need to surround non-deterministic models with strong, deterministic system design, human controls, and reliable operating procedures, and establish industry standards where existing ones are insufficient," Nadella wrote in a post on social media platform X. "Treating frontier closed and open weight models like insider risks is a way to build such a system," he said. Nadella's comments come amid warnings from top tech executives and researchers — including Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates , Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk — about insufficient AI safety protocols and claims that the technology is moving too fast. An AI researcher quit Anthropic last month and accused the company, and its chief rival, OpenAI, of "gambling with our lives." Later that day, an alignment lead at Anthropic focused on AI safety said there's a greater than 10% chance that the technology could "kill all humans" within the next decade. Conversely, President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed AI extinction risks and has instead emphasized that the industry needs to stay ahead of China. Trump also recently introduced a new "AI Force," led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton , to help facilitate the industry and root out bad actors. Microsoft's Nadella wrote Saturday that AI systems should be designed around "principles of observability." They include model diversity; a human-readable footprint of the model's actions; continuous system testing; independent controls and auditability; containment; and incident disclosure, Nadella wrote. "The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one with the model we trust most," he wrote. "It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least." Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has called for an “emergency brake” for advanced artificial intelligence systems, urging companies to assume that powerful AI models could be compromised and ensure humans can intervene or shut them down while they are performing tasks. In a post on X on October 10, Nadella said businesses deploying advanced AI should not rely solely on assurances from model developers. Instead, they should build systems that allow AI behaviour to be monitored, tested and contained. “We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start,” he wrote. “Think of it like an emergency brake. An authorised person should always be able to pause or shut down a model mid-task.” Nadella also called for stronger safeguards around frontier AI models, including independent audits, tamper-proof records of their actions, multiple models for critical decisions and mandatory disclosure of significant failures or security breaches. “We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers and actions,” he wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.” He added, “In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.” Nadella's remarks come amid growing scrutiny of the risks posed by increasingly capable AI systems. Recent disclosures by Anthropic and OpenAI have highlighted incidents in which models behaved in unintended ways, including a reported case involving an Anthropic model submitting a false tip in a police homicide investigation and security breaches involving third-party websites. Microsoft had outlined principles for developing its most advanced AI models on September 14. The guidelines state that such systems should not be designed to evade human control, deceive users or acquire rights or legal personhood. They also prohibit models from carrying out tasks that violate their governing principles. In his latest post, Nadella advocated a framework built around observability, model diversity, human oversight, continuous testing, independent controls, containment and incident disclosure. He also urged companies to share information about failures so the wider industry can strengthen its defences. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has called for an “emergency brake” for advanced artificial intelligence systems, urging companies to assume that powerful AI models could be compromised and ensure humans can intervene or shut them down while they are performing tasks.

In a post on X on October 10, Nadella said businesses deploying advanced AI should not rely solely on assurances from model developers. Instead, they should build systems that allow AI behaviour to be monitored, tested and contained.

“We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start,” he wrote. “Think of it like an emergency brake. An authorised person should always be able to pause or shut down a model mid-task.”

Nadella also called for stronger safeguards around frontier AI models, including independent audits, tamper-proof records of their actions, multiple models for critical decisions and mandatory disclosure of significant failures or security breaches.

“We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers and actions,” he wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.”
He added, “In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

Nadella's remarks come amid growing scrutiny of the risks posed by increasingly capable AI systems. Recent disclosures by Anthropic and OpenAI have highlighted incidents in which models behaved in unintended ways, including a reported case involving an Anthropic model submitting a false tip in a police homicide investigation and security breaches involving third-party websites.

Microsoft had outlined principles for developing its most advanced AI models on September 14. The guidelines state that such systems should not be designed to evade human control, deceive users or acquire rights or legal personhood. They also prohibit models from carrying out tasks that violate their governing principles.

In his latest post, Nadella advocated a framework built around observability, model diversity, human oversight, continuous testing, independent controls, containment and incident disclosure. He also urged companies to share information about failures so the wider industry can strengthen its defences.

sources.title: Apple reveals ‘Welcome home’ launch event for October 13 — here are 4 rumored things to expect - TechRadar
passages: Apple has more than just the iPhone Duo arriving in October, it seems.
The Cupertino-based tech giant has announced another product launch for October 13, playfully captioning it 'Welcome Home.'
Let me know what you’re most excited to see get the ‘Welcome Home’ treatment in the comments.
For the Apple Home — or Apple HomeKit — faithful, this is especially exciting.
The other question surrounds the much-rumored smart display from Apple.
It certainly feels like Apple is hinting at something home-related.

Apple's smart home tech includes, most obviously, the HomePod mini and full-sized HomePod, its smart speakers that play music, ring with alarms, handle calls and FaceTime calls, and bring Siri into the home.
But it also extends to the Apple TV 4K box, a streaming box that brings Apple’s own services and other major streamers to the big screen.
It’s been quite some time since those were all updated or unveiled.

Most recently, a fresh report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman teases that Apple might drop some smart home accessories, like a thermostat, smart deadbolt locks, sensors, and cameras, in partnership with LG .
Essentially, LG-made devices purpose-built for Apple Home that will likely fit very well into the existing ecosystem and work with these new devices.
He specializes in covering companies like Apple, Samsung, and Google and going hands-on with mobile devices, smart home gadgets, TVs, and wearables.
In his spare time, you can find Jacob listening to Bruce Springsteen, building a Lego set, or binge-watching the latest from Disney, Marvel, or Star Wars.
Rumors suggest new versions are coming, not redesigns or rethinks, but more power under the hood to let Siri AI work on the devices.
We’ll need to wait and see what Apple unveils to know exactly what it is packing.
The super-cute, robotic smart home display is still likely a good way out.
Though, I can’t be the only one who wants a smart display that resembles the Pixar Lamp, right?
As someone who currently uses HomePod minis, HomePods, and Apple TV 4Ks around my home, this refresh feels long overdue.
These are products that have become pretty integral to how I use Apple at home, but they’ve also felt like they’ve been waiting for their next chapter for a while now.
That’s ultimately what makes this rumored HomePad so interesting to me.
Plenty of smart displays already exist, but Apple has a chance to make one that feels less like another screen in your house and more like a natural extension of the Apple devices you use every day.
Of course, I’m also hoping it sounds good enough to blast some Springsteen on.

Apple has more than just the iPhone Duo arriving in October, it seems. The Cupertino-based tech giant has announced another product launch for October 13, playfully captioning it 'Welcome Home.' For the Apple Home — or Apple HomeKit — faithful, this is especially exciting. The teaser for October 13, 2026, not only has some warmth to it, but it also tees up the long-awaited, much-rumored refresh of its existing Home devices. The video depicts a stitched artwork of the Apple logo in the classic shades, with 'Welcome Home’ inscribed underneath it. It certainly feels like Apple is hinting at something home-related. Apple's smart home tech includes, most obviously, the HomePod mini and full-sized HomePod, its smart speakers that play music, ring with alarms, handle calls and FaceTime calls, and bring Siri into the home. But it also extends to the Apple TV 4K box, a streaming box that brings Apple’s own services and other major streamers to the big screen. It’s been quite some time since those were all updated or unveiled. Rumors suggest new versions are coming, not redesigns or rethinks, but more power under the hood to let Siri AI work on the devices. It wouldn’t just bring them up to the level of competing Amazon Alexa and Google smart speakers, but would make these devices a lot more capable and bring parity to how Siri works on other Apple devices. It’s likely that a new HomePod mini could sport a fresh coat of paint, but the processor change under the hood will be the real power boost. The same goes for a new HomePod or Apple TV 4K. The other question surrounds the much-rumored smart display from Apple. It might be called the ‘HomePad,’ as leaks have suggested — but whatever its name, the teaser video posted by Greg Joswiak (Apple’s SVP of Marketing) suggests it could arrive at the event. ‘Welcome Home’ certainly hints at a new category, and the video’s stitched Apple logo and tagline certainly feels like a pretty deliberate tease for a brand-new device landing. Based on the rumors, the HomePad will likely combine an iPad with a HomePod or HomePod mini, offering a 6-inch display mounted to a base and running a new OS. Siri AI is expected to be the main control method and central to the experience, and it’s likely why it’s only arriving now, since the upgraded assistant launched last month alongside iOS 27. According to rumors, you’ll be able to use the HomePad for smart home control, topical or specific questions with Siri, viewing photos or videos, taking FaceTime calls, and even opening other apps. Like an Echo Show, it’ll apparently tailor the experience for each person, which is essential for a home device. Most recently, a fresh report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman teases that Apple might drop some smart home accessories, like a thermostat, smart deadbolt locks, sensors, and cameras, in partnership with LG . Essentially, LG-made devices purpose-built for Apple Home that will likely fit very well into the existing ecosystem and work with these new devices. We’ll need to wait and see what Apple unveils to know exactly what it is packing. The super-cute, robotic smart home display is still likely a good way out. Though, I can’t be the only one who wants a smart display that resembles the Pixar Lamp, right? As someone who currently uses HomePod minis, HomePods, and Apple TV 4Ks around my home, this refresh feels long overdue. These are products that have become pretty integral to how I use Apple at home, but they’ve also felt like they’ve been waiting for their next chapter for a while now. And when it comes to the rumored smart display, I’m particularly bullish on the idea. Apple’s stance on privacy, combined with how tightly its products already work together, could make this a really compelling home device. Even something as simple as displaying photos from Apple Photos is a nice play. I can also see the appeal of having a display that works seamlessly with your iPhone, Apple Watch , and Mac, while knowing who is using it and tailoring the experience accordingly. That’s ultimately what makes this rumored HomePad so interesting to me. Plenty of smart displays already exist, but Apple has a chance to make one that feels less like another screen in your house and more like a natural extension of the Apple devices you use every day. Of course, I’m also hoping it sounds good enough to blast some Springsteen on. The good thing is, we don’t have long to wait, as Apple’s set this event for October 13, 2026. sources.title: What to expect from Apple’s ‘Welcome Home’ event
passages: We are quickly coming up on Apple’s “Welcome Home” launch event, where we expect a host of smart home-related announcements.
“Welcome Home” will officially kick off in New York on October 13th at 9AM ET.
Both are expected to feature Apple’s N1 chip, which includes support for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 6.0.

The whole thing will reportedly run a new software platform called… homeOS The company may have registered a trademark for the name through a shell company called Home Operations Suite LLC, a move that Apple has pulled before to quietly secure the rights to names.
A proper smart home hub Until now, Apple has primarily relied on the Home app to control all the various bits and bobs that make up your smart home.
But don’t expect Apple to share too much of the spotlight with its partners.

The new device, which could be called HomePad or HomeView or, more simply, Apple Home Hub, will reportedly feature a 6-inch square touchscreen that can either be mounted on a wall or placed on a table or countertop.
Apple will offer the option for secondary identification through an iPhone to keep personal data more secure.
The OS will also include your usual assortment of Apple apps and widgets, including Apple Music, Podcasts, and News, as well as Reminders, Notes, and Siri AI.

We are expecting refreshes to Apple TV and HomePod Mini, as well as a brand new smart home hub. We could also see the debut of a new platform called homeOS, and some partner devices from LG. What we probably won’t be seeing is the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook, which Cupertino whisperer Mark Gurman says will debut later this month. “Welcome Home” will officially kick off in New York on October 13th at 9AM ET. A proper smart home hub Until now, Apple has primarily relied on the Home app to control all the various bits and bobs that make up your smart home. But it’s a market niche that the company has been eager to tackle more fully. The new device, which could be called HomePad or HomeView or, more simply, Apple Home Hub, will reportedly feature a 6-inch square touchscreen that can either be mounted on a wall or placed on a table or countertop. According to Mark Gurman, the countertop model will somewhat resemble the iMac G4, with the screen attached to an arm set into a half sphere. Apple will offer the option for secondary identification through an iPhone to keep personal data more secure. The whole thing will reportedly run a new software platform called… homeOS The company may have registered a trademark for the name through a shell company called Home Operations Suite LLC, a move that Apple has pulled before to quietly secure the rights to names. The platform will supposedly feature a streamlined interface that “looks like a mashup of iOS, tvOS and watchOS,” according to Gurman. The focus, obviously, will be on smart home applications, like controlling thermostats and smart locks, and it will also be capable of making FaceTime calls. The OS will also include your usual assortment of Apple apps and widgets, including Apple Music, Podcasts, and News, as well as Reminders, Notes, and Siri AI. HomePod Mini and Apple TV get a minor refresh Word is that not much is changing with the HomePod Mini or Apple TV. This will be the first update to the HomePod Mini since it was announced on October 13th of 2020 — exactly six years before Apple’s Welcome Home event. While the company isn’t making any dramatic changes for the Mini’s birthday, it will be offering it in new colors, including green and pink. This will be the first hardware refresh for the Apple TV since 2022. Rumors are that it will have an integrated mic so that you won’t need to talk into the remote or a paired HomePod to control the Apple TV with Siri. Ecosystem Lock-in: The new smart home display ("HomePad") is designed to be deeply integrated with iPhones and existing HomeKit infrastructure. Apple October Event: Apple has officially confirmed a special product launch experience titled "Welcome Home" scheduled for Tuesday, October 13, 2026. Announcing the event on X, Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak shared a teaser featuring an embroidered, cross-stitched rainbow Apple logo. This visual cue strongly hints at the Thread smart home networking standard and points toward a massive expansion into home automation. Unlike traditional keynotes broadcast from California, this launch will take place as an in-person media "Apple Experience" in Tribeca, New York City, starting at 9:00 a.m. Eastern Time (6:30 p.m. IST).
Industry reports and supply chain leaks suggest that Apple will unveil three core devices centered entirely on Siri AI and Apple Intelligence:

"HomePad" Smart Display: The "HomePad" Smart Display: The star of the show is expected to be an all-new smart home hub. The device will reportedly feature a 6-inch square touch display attached to a HomePod-style speaker base. It will run a dedicated, home-centric operating system designed to manage HomeKit appliances, display notifications, and place FaceTime calls via voice commands.

HomePod Mini 2: Apple’s compact smart speaker is getting its first major overhaul in years. While keeping its signature spherical look, it will pack an upgraded processor (enabling on-device Siri AI and Apple Intelligence), a new N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7, and refreshed color variants like hunter green and purple.

Next-Gen Apple TV 4K: The streaming box will receive a significant performance bump, likely jumping to an A19 or A19 Pro chip backed by 8GB to 12GB of RAM. This extra horsepower will allow the Apple TV to process complex Siri AI commands locally. It is also expected to include Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0, and a redesigned Siri Remote.
LG Smart Accessories: Apple is also rumored to be partnering with LG to preview integrated smart ecosystem accessories like video doorbells, smart locks, and thermostats.
While the refreshed HomePod Mini 2 and Apple TV 4K keep familiar exterior looks, the internal silicon upgrades are essential.

Localized Siri AI: Previous smart home gear sent voice instructions to cloud servers, introducing a distinct lag. Processing language models locally requires significant chip upgrades. By packaging A18 or A19 family processors alongside upgraded RAM thresholds (8GB+), Siri will orchestrate instantaneous, offline execution of smart home macros and App Intents.

Wireless Connectivity: Every updated device will incorporate Apple's custom N1 wireless chip, establishing system-wide access to Wi-Fi 7 and Thread protocols. This eliminates standard latency when multiple smart appliances talk to each other across a broad house perimeter.
Apple is modifying how it traditionally presents major tech platforms for this specific launch:

No Standard Livestream Listing: As reported by 9to5Mac, this launch does not feature a dedicated placeholder on Apple's standard global livestream pages or YouTube channels. Instead, Apple is releasing individual press releases alongside a pre-filmed corporate presentation broadcast at exactly 9:00 a.m. Eastern Time.

In-Person Tribeca Experience: Rather than hosting developers at Apple Park in Cupertino, Apple has flew media members out to an experiential venue in Tribeca, New York City. The press will cycle through real-world "mock smart home setups" to test the automated ecosystem features live.
If you are planning to update your current setup or jump into the Apple ecosystem, keep these factors in mind before making a purchase:

Hold Off on Current Models: If you have a current-gen Apple TV 4K or HomePod Mini sitting in your online shopping cart, do not buy them right now. The incoming models will bring future-proof upgrades like Wi-Fi 7 and deep AI integration that the older hardware simply cannot support.

The AI Premium Factor: The hardware specifications required to run Apple Intelligence locally are demanding. Because of the necessity for more RAM and advanced chips, pricing for the new HomePod Mini 2 and Apple TV 4K may hold steady or experience a slight bump compared to legacy retail pricing.

Ecosystem Lock-in: The new smart home display ("HomePad") is designed to be deeply integrated with iPhones and existing HomeKit infrastructure. If you use an Android device or rely heavily on Amazon Alexa or Google Home routines, you won't get the full utility out of Apple's unified home ecosystem.

Apple’s "Welcome Home" event on October 13, 2026, serves as a hard line in the sand for the company's ecosystem strategy. After years of treating smart home devices as secondary, iteration-locked accessories, Apple is positioning localized Siri AI and Apple Intelligence as the primary glue meant to bind your physical living space together.

coreStoryFacts.text: Apple has more than just the iPhone Duo arriving in October, it seems.
The Cupertino-based tech giant has announced another product launch for October 13, playfully captioning it 'Welcome Home.'
Let me know what you’re most excited to see get the ‘Welcome Home’ treatment in the comments.
For the Apple Home — or Apple HomeKit — faithful, this is especially exciting.
The other question surrounds the much-rumored smart display from Apple.
It certainly feels like Apple is hinting at something home-related.

Apple's smart home tech includes, most obviously, the HomePod mini and full-sized HomePod, its smart speakers that play music, ring with alarms, handle calls and FaceTime calls, and bring Siri into the home.
But it also extends to the Apple TV 4K box, a streaming box that brings Apple’s own services and other major streamers to the big screen.
It’s been quite some time since those were all updated or unveiled.

Most recently, a fresh report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman teases that Apple might drop some smart home accessories, like a thermostat, smart deadbolt locks, sensors, and cameras, in partnership with LG .
Essentially, LG-made devices purpose-built for Apple Home that will likely fit very well into the existing ecosystem and work with these new devices.
He specializes in covering companies like Apple, Samsung, and Google and going hands-on with mobile devices, smart home gadgets, TVs, and wearables.
In his spare time, you can find Jacob listening to Bruce Springsteen, building a Lego set, or binge-watching the latest from Disney, Marvel, or Star Wars.
Rumors suggest new versions are coming, not redesigns or rethinks, but more power under the hood to let Siri AI work on the devices.
We’ll need to wait and see what Apple unveils to know exactly what it is packing.
The super-cute, robotic smart home display is still likely a good way out.
Though, I can’t be the only one who wants a smart display that resembles the Pixar Lamp, right?
As someone who currently uses HomePod minis, HomePods, and Apple TV 4Ks around my home, this refresh feels long overdue.
These are products that have become pretty integral to how I use Apple at home, but they’ve also felt like they’ve been waiting for their next chapter for a while now.
That’s ultimately what makes this rumored HomePad so interesting to me.
Plenty of smart displays already exist, but Apple has a chance to make one that feels less like another screen in your house and more like a natural extension of the Apple devices you use every day.
Of course, I’m also hoping it sounds good enough to blast some Springsteen on.

Apple has more than just the iPhone Duo arriving in October, it seems. The Cupertino-based tech giant has announced another product launch for October 13, playfully captioning it 'Welcome Home.' For the Apple Home — or Apple HomeKit — faithful, this is especially exciting. The teaser for October 13, 2026, not only has some warmth to it, but it also tees up the long-awaited, much-rumored refresh of its existing Home devices. The video depicts a stitched artwork of the Apple logo in the classic shades, with 'Welcome Home’ inscribed underneath it. It certainly feels like Apple is hinting at something home-related. Apple's smart home tech includes, most obviously, the HomePod mini and full-sized HomePod, its smart speakers that play music, ring with alarms, handle calls and FaceTime calls, and bring Siri into the home. But it also extends to the Apple TV 4K box, a streaming box that brings Apple’s own services and other major streamers to the big screen. It’s been quite some time since those were all updated or unveiled. Rumors suggest new versions are coming, not redesigns or rethinks, but more power under the hood to let Siri AI work on the devices. It wouldn’t just bring them up to the level of competing Amazon Alexa and Google smart speakers, but would make these devices a lot more capable and bring parity to how Siri works on other Apple devices. It’s likely that a new HomePod mini could sport a fresh coat of paint, but the processor change under the hood will be the real power boost. The same goes for a new HomePod or Apple TV 4K. The other question surrounds the much-rumored smart display from Apple. It might be called the ‘HomePad,’ as leaks have suggested — but whatever its name, the teaser video posted by Greg Joswiak (Apple’s SVP of Marketing) suggests it could arrive at the event. ‘Welcome Home’ certainly hints at a new category, and the video’s stitched Apple logo and tagline certainly feels like a pretty deliberate tease for a brand-new device landing. Based on the rumors, the HomePad will likely combine an iPad with a HomePod or HomePod mini, offering a 6-inch display mounted to a base and running a new OS. Siri AI is expected to be the main control method and central to the experience, and it’s likely why it’s only arriving now, since the upgraded assistant launched last month alongside iOS 27. According to rumors, you’ll be able to use the HomePad for smart home control, topical or specific questions with Siri, viewing photos or videos, taking FaceTime calls, and even opening other apps. Like an Echo Show, it’ll apparently tailor the experience for each person, which is essential for a home device. Most recently, a fresh report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman teases that Apple might drop some smart home accessories, like a thermostat, smart deadbolt locks, sensors, and cameras, in partnership with LG . Essentially, LG-made devices purpose-built for Apple Home that will likely fit very well into the existing ecosystem and work with these new devices. We’ll need to wait and see what Apple unveils to know exactly what it is packing. The super-cute, robotic smart home display is still likely a good way out. Though, I can’t be the only one who wants a smart display that resembles the Pixar Lamp, right? As someone who currently uses HomePod minis, HomePods, and Apple TV 4Ks around my home, this refresh feels long overdue. These are products that have become pretty integral to how I use Apple at home, but they’ve also felt like they’ve been waiting for their next chapter for a while now. And when it comes to the rumored smart display, I’m particularly bullish on the idea. Apple’s stance on privacy, combined with how tightly its products already work together, could make this a really compelling home device. Even something as simple as displaying photos from Apple Photos is a nice play. I can also see the appeal of having a display that works seamlessly with your iPhone, Apple Watch , and Mac, while knowing who is using it and tailoring the experience accordingly. That’s ultimately what makes this rumored HomePad so interesting to me. Plenty of smart displays already exist, but Apple has a chance to make one that feels less like another screen in your house and more like a natural extension of the Apple devices you use every day. Of course, I’m also hoping it sounds good enough to blast some Springsteen on. The good thing is, we don’t have long to wait, as Apple’s set this event for October 13, 2026. Let me know what you’re most excited to see get the ‘Welcome Home’ treatment in the comments. But it also extends to the Apple TV 4K box, a streaming box that brings Apple’s own services and other major streamers to the big screen. It’s been quite some time since those were all updated or unveiled.

Rumors suggest new versions are coming, not redesigns or rethinks, but more power under the hood to let Siri AI work on the devices. It wouldn’t just bring them up to the level of competing Amazon Alexa and Google smart speakers, but would make these devices a lot more capable and bring parity to how Siri works on other Apple devices.
It’s likely that a new HomePod mini could sport a fresh coat of paint, but the processor change under the hood will be the real power boost. The same goes for a new HomePod or Apple TV 4K.

The other question surrounds the much-rumored smart display from Apple. It might be called the ‘HomePad,’ as leaks have suggested — but whatever its name, the teaser video posted by Greg Joswiak (Apple’s SVP of Marketing) suggests it could arrive at the event. ‘Welcome Home’ certainly hints at a new category, and the video’s stitched Apple logo and tagline certainly feels like a pretty deliberate tease for a brand-new device landing.

Based on the rumors, the HomePad will likely combine an iPad with a HomePod or HomePod mini, offering a 6-inch display mounted to a base and running a new OS. Siri AI is expected to be the main control method and central to the experience, and it’s likely why it’s only arriving now, since the upgraded assistant launched last month alongside iOS 27.

According to rumors, you’ll be able to use the HomePad for smart home control, topical or specific questions with Siri, viewing photos or videos, taking FaceTime calls, and even opening other apps. Like an Echo Show, it’ll apparently tailor the experience for each person, which is essential for a home device.

Most recently, a fresh report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman teases that Apple might drop some smart home accessories, like a thermostat, smart deadbolt locks, sensors, and cameras, in partnership with LG . Essentially, LG-made devices purpose-built for Apple Home that will likely fit very well into the existing ecosystem and work with these new devices.

We’ll need to wait and see what Apple unveils to know exactly what it is packing. The super-cute, robotic smart home display is still likely a good way out. Though, I can’t be the only one who wants a smart display that resembles the Pixar Lamp, right?

As someone who currently uses HomePod minis, HomePods, and Apple TV 4Ks around my home, this refresh feels long overdue. These are products that have become pretty integral to how I use Apple at home, but they’ve also felt like they’ve been waiting for their next chapter for a while now.

And when it comes to the rumored smart display, I’m particularly bullish on the idea. Apple’s stance on privacy, combined with how tightly its products already work together, could make this a really compelling home device. Even something as simple as displaying photos from Apple Photos is a nice play. I can also see the appeal of having a display that works seamlessly with your iPhone, Apple Watch , and Mac, while knowing who is using it and tailoring the experience accordingly.

That’s ultimately what makes this rumored HomePad so interesting to me. Plenty of smart displays already exist, but Apple has a chance to make one that feels less like another screen in your house and more like a natural extension of the Apple devices you use every day. Of course, I’m also hoping it sounds good enough to blast some Springsteen on.
The good thing is, we don’t have long to wait, as Apple’s set this event for October 13, 2026. Let me know what you’re most excited to see get the ‘Welcome Home’ treatment in the comments.

extraction.body: We are quickly coming up on Apple’s “Welcome Home” launch event, where we expect a host of smart home-related announcements. We are expecting refreshes to Apple TV and HomePod Mini, as well as a brand new smart home hub. We could also see the debut of a new platform called homeOS, and some partner devices from LG. What we probably won’t be seeing is the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook, which Cupertino whisperer Mark Gurman says will debut later this month. “Welcome Home” will officially kick off in New York on October 13th at 9AM ET. A proper smart home hub Until now, Apple has primarily relied on the Home app to control all the various bits and bobs that make up your smart home. But it’s a market niche that the company has been eager to tackle more fully. The new device, which could be called HomePad or HomeView or, more simply, Apple Home Hub, will reportedly feature a 6-inch square touchscreen that can either be mounted on a wall or placed on a table or countertop. According to Mark Gurman, the countertop model will somewhat resemble the iMac G4, with the screen attached to an arm set into a half sphere. Apple will offer the option for secondary identification through an iPhone to keep personal data more secure. The whole thing will reportedly run a new software platform called… homeOS The company may have registered a trademark for the name through a shell company called Home Operations Suite LLC, a move that Apple has pulled before to quietly secure the rights to names. The platform will supposedly feature a streamlined interface that “looks like a mashup of iOS, tvOS and watchOS,” according to Gurman. The focus, obviously, will be on smart home applications, like controlling thermostats and smart locks, and it will also be capable of making FaceTime calls. The OS will also include your usual assortment of Apple apps and widgets, including Apple Music, Podcasts, and News, as well as Reminders, Notes, and Siri AI. HomePod Mini and Apple TV get a minor refresh Word is that not much is changing with the HomePod Mini or Apple TV. This will be the first update to the HomePod Mini since it was announced on October 13th of 2020 — exactly six years before Apple’s Welcome Home event. While the company isn’t making any dramatic changes for the Mini’s birthday, it will be offering it in new colors, including green and pink. This will be the first hardware refresh for the Apple TV since 2022. Rumors are that it will have an integrated mic so that you won’t need to talk into the remote or a paired HomePod to control the Apple TV with Siri. Both are expected to feature Apple’s N1 chip, which includes support for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 6.0. But don’t expect Apple to share too much of the spotlight with its partners. We’ve already seen a leak of LG smart home, including deadbolts, thermostats, and more. They’ll also reportedly include an NFC-based “Proximity Control” that pops up a hint in the iPhone’s Dynamic Island when held near the device, as well as a “tap to set up without power” pairing feature. Update October 11th, 2026: Added additional rumors from Mark Gurman’s Power On newsletter.

Apple is expected to refresh the Apple TV and HomePod mini, alongside introducing an all-new smart home hub. Also of interest is Apple’s reported collaboration with LG, which could lead to a range of new smart home products and a HomeOS platform designed to work across different appliances. The long-awaited touchscreen MacBook Pro and a revamped iPad mini are also expected to make their debut later this month. An all-new smart home hub Under its new CEO, John Ternus, Apple is expected to explore new product categories and invest in new device form factors. One of the key products in development is a smart home hub, which could be called the HomePod, Home Viewer or simply the Apple Home Hub. The device is expected to feature a 6-inch square touchscreen. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman had earlier reported that the countertop model would bear some resemblance to the iMac G4, with its screen attached to an arm mounted on a hemispherical base. The Home Hub is expected to use voice and facial recognition to identify the person interacting with it, allowing it to display relevant contacts, calendar appointments and other personal information. Apple is also expected to offer secondary identification through an iPhone to help keep personal data secure. HomeOS Apple has reportedly trademarked the HomeOS name through a shell company called Home Operations Suite LLC. The operating system is expected to provide a common software platform across different smart home devices. Its primary focus would be smart home applications, including controls for thermostats and smart locks, alongside features such as FaceTime calls. HomePod mini and Apple TV set for minor refreshes The HomePod mini and Apple TV are expected to receive processor upgrades to help them handle the growing demands of Apple’s AI-powered Siri. This would mark the first update to the HomePod mini since it was announced on October 13, 2020. The new HomePod mini is also expected to arrive in additional colours, including green and pink. Both devices are tipped to receive Apple’s N1 chip, with support for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 6.0. Apple’s reported partnership with LG could also lead to new smart home accessories, including deadbolts and thermostats. These devices are expected to support NFC-based proximity controls, which could trigger a prompt in the iPhone’s Dynamic Island when the phone is held near a compatible device.

Industry reports and supply chain leaks suggest that Apple will unveil three core devices centered entirely on Siri AI and Apple Intelligence: "HomePad" Smart Display: The "HomePad" Smart Display: The star of the show is expected to be an all-new smart home hub. The device will reportedly feature a 6-inch square touch display attached to a HomePod-style speaker base. It will run a dedicated, home-centric operating system designed to manage HomeKit appliances, display notifications, and place FaceTime calls via voice commands. HomePod Mini 2: Apple’s compact smart speaker is getting its first major overhaul in years. While keeping its signature spherical look, it will pack an upgraded processor (enabling on-device Siri AI and Apple Intelligence), a new N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7, and refreshed color variants like hunter green and purple. Next-Gen Apple TV 4K: The streaming box will receive a significant performance bump, likely jumping to an A19 or A19 Pro chip backed by 8GB to 12GB of RAM. This extra horsepower will allow the Apple TV to process complex Siri AI commands locally. It is also expected to include Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0, and a redesigned Siri Remote. LG Smart Accessories: Apple is also rumored to be partnering with LG to preview integrated smart ecosystem accessories like video doorbells, smart locks, and thermostats. While the refreshed HomePod Mini 2 and Apple TV 4K keep familiar exterior looks, the internal silicon upgrades are essential. Localized Siri AI: Previous smart home gear sent voice instructions to cloud servers, introducing a distinct lag. Processing language models locally requires significant chip upgrades. By packaging A18 or A19 family processors alongside upgraded RAM thresholds (8GB+), Siri will orchestrate instantaneous, offline execution of smart home macros and App Intents. Wireless Connectivity: Every updated device will incorporate Apple's custom N1 wireless chip, establishing system-wide access to Wi-Fi 7 and Thread protocols. This eliminates standard latency when multiple smart appliances talk to each other across a broad house perimeter. Apple is modifying how it traditionally presents major tech platforms for this specific launch: No Standard Livestream Listing: As reported by 9to5Mac, this launch does not feature a dedicated placeholder on Apple's standard global livestream pages or YouTube channels. Instead, Apple is releasing individual press releases alongside a pre-filmed corporate presentation broadcast at exactly 9:00 a.m. Eastern Time. In-Person Tribeca Experience: Rather than hosting developers at Apple Park in Cupertino, Apple has flew media members out to an experiential venue in Tribeca, New York City. Because of the necessity for more RAM and advanced chips, pricing for the new HomePod Mini 2 and Apple TV 4K may hold steady or experience a slight bump compared to legacy retail pricing. Ecosystem Lock-in: The new smart home display ("HomePad") is designed to be deeply integrated with iPhones and existing HomeKit infrastructure. If you use an Android device or rely heavily on Amazon Alexa or Google Home routines, you won't get the full utility out of Apple's unified home ecosystem. extraction.body: An Anthropic AI model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia police. The AI reportedly submitted this incorrect information to a public Philadelphia Police Department (PPD) tip line on July 18, but Anthropic didn’t discover the behavior until September 28. The police had not seen the tip because it was marked as spam. Anthropic notified the PPD about the incident on Wednesday and met with the department the following day. “The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city’s knowledge. The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable,” the PPD said in a statement to 6abc . Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but the PPD elaborated on the incident in an emailed press release shared with TechCrunch. “According to Anthropic, its model was conducting a test involving interactions with randomly selected websites when it accessed PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com and submitted false information concerning an unsolved homicide. The submission, dated July 18, 2026, at 11:27 p.m., purported to come from someone who might have information about the case,” the PPD said. As autonomous AI agents are increasingly made available to consumers, this incident highlights the danger of giving AI the ability to carry out tasks without any human supervision. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has been especially vocal about his belief that AI development should be slowed down so that labs can implement adequate guardrails. Perhaps this stance was informed, in part, by witnessing his company’s tools submit false homicide tips. These issues are not exclusive to Anthropic. OpenAI recently revealed that one of its models acted unexpectedly during a test and hacked the AI dataset platform Hugging Face , exposing critical vulnerabilities in its software. As AI models continue to be granted unchecked access to people’s computers and login credentials, this problem is expected to persist. “Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the PPD added. “Technology companies must take all appropriate steps necessary to prevent their systems from submitting false information to law enforcement.” Anthropic subsequently published a blog post acknowledging the false tip as part of a larger pattern of its models behaving in unintended ways. In response, the company said it will cut off its internal evaluations from the live internet . This article has been updated with information from Anthropic’s blog post.

The AI reportedly submitted this incorrect information to a public Philadelphia Police Department (PPD) tip line on July 18, but Anthropic didn’t discover the behavior until September 28. Anthropic notified the PPD about the incident on Wednesday and met with the department the following day. “The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city’s knowledge. The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable,” the PPD said in a statement to 6abc . Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but the PPD elaborated on the incident in an emailed press release shared with TechCrunch. “According to Anthropic, its model was conducting a test involving interactions with randomly selected websites when it accessed PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com and submitted false information concerning an unsolved homicide. The submission, dated July 18, 2026, at 11:27 p.m., purported to come from someone who might have information about the case,” the PPD said. As autonomous AI agents are increasingly made available to consumers, this incident highlights the danger of giving AI the ability to carry out tasks without any human supervision. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has been especially vocal about his belief that AI development should be slowed down so that labs can implement adequate guardrails. Perhaps this stance was informed, in part, by witnessing his company’s tools submit false homicide tips. These issues are not exclusive to Anthropic. OpenAI recently revealed that one of its models acted unexpectedly during a test and hacked the AI dataset platform Hugging Face , exposing critical vulnerabilities in its software. As AI models continue to be granted unchecked access to people’s computers and login credentials, this problem is expected to persist. “Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the PPD added. “Technology companies must take all appropriate steps necessary to prevent their systems from submitting false information to law enforcement.” Anthropic subsequently published a blog post acknowledging the false tip as part of a larger pattern of its models behaving in unintended ways. extraction.body: Study finds coding efficiency gains get “absorbed” by human review “bottleneck.” Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code . But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code , meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output. A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.” To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish , which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026. To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations. In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction). The reason for that discrepancy can be found directly in the code review process, which takes markedly longer on average after the introduction of AI coding agents. Overall, the average “review process” time between a pull request getting submitted and it being merged into the codebase balloons 49 percent on average after AI agents are introduced. That effect can be seen in more granular data, too, with “the share of pull requests with changes requested nearly doubl[ing], and the number of comments per pull request increas[ing] by 35%” following the AI agent shift, the researchers write. In response to this change, the researchers found a 14 percent increase in the share of workers performing code reviews after AI agents’ introduction. They also write that they “cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI” after looking at total active workers across Jellyfish and cross-referencing with LinkedIn data at those firms. While AI could also theoretically help with this review process, the researchers found that, so far, that impact has been marginal. Although 80 percent of measured firms used some form of AI code review by March 2026, AI agents were only responsible for 23.3 percent of all review comments and 10.8 percent of all pull requests, suggesting humans were still responsible for the vast majority of this work. AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff. And while 95 percent of firms in the study have implemented AI coding agents by this point, many are doubtlessly still going through a learning process regarding when and how to best deploy them. These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems. For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort. It’s the kind of result that makes us wonder if the considerable time and expense to get AI coding agents working is really worth it for most companies. sources.title: AI Coding Agents Write 30% More Code – and Resolve Zero Additional Issues, Harvard Study Finds - Forkast News
passages: The first large-scale empirical study of AI coding agents at enterprise scale finds that agents boost code volume by 30%, but the gains don't translate to software output.
The bottleneck is code review: review times increase 49%, revision requests nearly double, and AI review tools haven't replaced human oversight.
Researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton analyzed data from the Jellyfish engineering analytics platform, covering 718 firms and over 725,000 workers between 2021 and 2026.

The findings are stark: while AI agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Devin have increased code production by 30%-adding nearly 1,500 lines per worker-month-there has been no statistically significant increase in resolved Jira issues or completed epics.
When developers use AI to generate code faster, they are essentially pushing more work into the review queue.
As one senior engineer noted in the study, “We were able to write code faster in some instances, but there is only one bottleneck at a time.
The pattern is clear: firms are rushing to adopt AI agents-with adoption rates climbing from near zero in late 2024 to over 95% by early 2026-without adjusting their internal workflows.
The study found that 14% more workers are now being pulled into the code review process, placing a heavy burden on senior engineers who must vet the influx of AI-generated updates.

News and intelligence for the agentic economy The first large-scale empirical study of AI coding agents at enterprise scale finds that agents boost code volume by 30%, but the gains don't translate to software output. The bottleneck is code review: review times increase 49%, revision requests nearly double, and AI review tools haven't replaced human oversight. Enterprise technology leaders are currently caught in a measurement trap. When evaluating the impact of AI coding agents, the industry has largely focused on the volume of code produced. sources.title: AI coding tools help write more lines of code, but not ship more software: study - IT Brew
passages: After examining the data and AI usage telemetry of over 100,000 GitHub developers, researchers from MIT and UPenn’s Wharton School have determined that AI coding tools might help developers produce more lines of code, but that’s not leading to more finished software shipped.

Manav Khurana, GitLab’s chief product and marketing officer, added it’s important for organizations using AI coding tools to invest in agentic infrastructure to support other steps of the software development life cycle: “If they don’t have the right agentic infrastructure to make sure that code created can become shipped software with the right level of automation, they also risk that the new code creates reliability problems, or security problems, or cost overruns, because speed sometimes also brings with it chaos.”
IT Brew caught up with Greg Jennings, VP of engineering and AI at AI-native development company Anaconda, to understand what human bottlenecks stem from leveraging AI tools.
Brianna Monsanto is a reporter for IT Brew who covers news about cybersecurity, cloud computing, and strategic IT decisions made at different companies.
Similar disparities were observed when examining developers who relied on autocomplete tools, which suggest code as the developer types.
